decision: User-selected main scenario list: 12 per depth. Six per depth are forced family anchors (one per family, 30 total, one per creature profile); six per depth are free, iconic picks with no family requirement. Entries are incidents, malware families and documented technique variants, not CVEs. Sources establish the victim action; family assignment of anchors is an editorial browsing choice. status: sourced = a source for the victim action was fetched and read; partial = occurrence and part of the victim action sourced, with the gap stated in note; unsupported = research did not find evidence for this depth/placement (see note; not yet reclassified); needs-sources = named in research with no source recorded yet; provisional = reporting establishes phishing but not that a password alone was enough.

sunlight.name: Follina
sunlight.victimAction: Open a malicious document (document-opening variant only; preview routes are separate)

sunlight.name: Carbanak
sunlight.victimAction: A bank employee opens a malicious attachment

sunlight.name: PC Cyborg / AIDS Trojan
sunlight.victimAction: Load and run a mailed 'AIDS Information' diskette
sunlight.note: Primary source is the US DOE CIAC bulletin A-10 (19 Dec 1989), served only over plain HTTP so it is not linked as a source: http://ftp.cerias.purdue.edu/pub/advisories/ciac/a-fy90/a-10.ciac-cyborg-trojan-horse . It states the trojan arrived on a mailed "AIDS Information Introductory Diskette" and asks anyone who ran the disk to call CIAC. Delivery was physical post, not email. An HTTPS source has not been found yet.

sunlight.name: Emotet (attachment route)
sunlight.victimAction: Open a malicious Word attachment and enable its macros

sunlight.name: RSA SecurID (Excel attachment)
sunlight.victimAction: Retrieve a phishing email from the junk folder and open its Excel attachment

sunlight.name: CryptoLocker (email-attachment route)
sunlight.victimAction: Open a zipped email attachment and run the executable inside
sunlight.note: Email-attachment delivery is established; neither source states the user-opening step explicitly (CISA only advises 'use caution when opening email attachments'). SecureWorks says Gameover Zeus (Upatre ZIP attachment), not direct spam, became the primary distribution route from Oct 2013. The 'email-attachment route' label is fair for early versions.

twilight.name: 0ktapus
twilight.victimAction: Enter credentials and authentication codes on a phishing site

twilight.name: Uber
twilight.victimAction: A contractor accepts an attacker-induced MFA request

twilight.name: Tycoon2FA
twilight.victimAction: Complete MFA through the mass-phishing campaign's interception branch

twilight.name: Retool
twilight.victimAction: A provider employee discloses MFA codes, enabling downstream account takeovers

twilight.name: Dropbox
twilight.victimAction: An employee supplies an OTP to a fake CircleCI login page

twilight.name: Scattered Spider
twilight.victimAction: Disclose an OTP or approve an MFA push (no single universal entry route)

twilight.name: Twitter (2020 employee MFA compromise)
twilight.victimAction: Employees enter credentials on a vishing-linked phishing site and some approve the resulting MFA request

twilight.name: Cisco (2022 MFA approval)
twilight.victimAction: Accept an attacker-initiated MFA push after vishing calls

twilight.name: Reddit (second-factor phishing)
twilight.victimAction: Enter credentials (and a second-factor token) on a cloned intranet login page
twilight.note: Reddit's own post (reddit.com) returned a JS challenge and could not be read; redditinc.com summary only says 'obtaining one employee's credentials' with no second-factor detail. Second factor was the attacker's stated aim; Register adds the phished employee had MFA enabled, implying a token was relayed, but no source explicitly says the employee typed a token. Year 2023 confirmed (5 Feb 2023).

twilight.name: EvilProxy (MFA-phishing campaigns)
twilight.victimAction: Sign in (including MFA) on a reverse-proxy phishing page that relays to the real login

twilight.name: Midnight Blizzard (Teams-induced MFA approvals)
twilight.victimAction: Enter an attacker-supplied number-matching code into Microsoft Authenticator after a Teams lure
twilight.note: Occurred and Teams lure confirmed. But the detailed flow is code-entry (number matching), not a plain approve-tap: the attacker shows a code, the user types it into Authenticator. Microsoft's summary line says 'approval of MFA prompts', so the original string is loosely supported; the corrected string is more precise. Campaign affected fewer than 40 organisations.

midnight.name: John Podesta
midnight.victimAction: Submit a password on a password-reset phishing page

midnight.name: The Onion
midnight.victimAction: Submit credentials to a phishing page

midnight.name: Twitter "Stalkers app" scam
midnight.victimAction: Submit a password to a fake app, so accounts can be used for further promotion and spam

midnight.name: PyPI / JuiceLedger
midnight.victimAction: A maintainer submits a password (scope: only accounts without additional MFA)

midnight.name: Ryan Collins Apple / Google phishing
midnight.victimAction: Submit a password, giving access to private accounts
midnight.note: Occurrence and password submission are established (>=50 iCloud and 72 Gmail accounts; Nov 2012-Sep 2014). No fetched source says whether victim accounts had two-step verification, so password-ONLY is unestablished, not disproved. DOJ press releases and the sentencing memo could not be extracted (blocked or empty), so none are cited. Keep Midnight placement only with that caveat or find the memo text.

midnight.name: Instagram account-ransom campaign
midnight.victimAction: Submit a password; the account is taken over and a payment demanded for its return

midnight.name: Associated Press phishing
midnight.victimAction: Staff are lured to a fake login page asking for corporate network credentials; AP Twitter accounts were then hijacked (public reporting does not document how the Twitter password itself was obtained)
midnight.note: AP confirmed the hack was preceded by phishing on its corporate network, but the quoted internal memo only warns staff ('If you have already ... entered your logon credentials, contact the help desk'); no source confirms a victim submitted a password or that the Twitter password was the credential taken. Twitter had no 2FA until 22 May 2013 (after the 23 Apr hack), so Twitter-side password-only is plausible (researcher inference). AP's own article returned HTTP 403, so not cited.

midnight.name: Guardian phishing
midnight.victimAction: Click a phishing email link to a fake login page and submit a password (Guardian Twitter accounts then hijacked)
midnight.note: Occurrence and phishing method are established, but the sources describe the SEA's general method; none documents which Guardian staff entered what, or that no extra factor applied. Twitter offered no 2FA until 22 May 2013 (Ars, see AP entry), after this April 2013 incident, so password-only for the Twitter accounts is a reasonable inference, not stated reporting.

midnight.name: Financial Times phishing
midnight.victimAction: Submit a corporate Google Apps password on a fake login page (Twitter and blog access followed from the compromised email accounts)

midnight.name: Colin Powell phishing
midnight.victimAction: Click a spoofed Google security-alert link (the same Bit.ly campaign that hit Podesta); password submission and absence of 2FA are not documented
midnight.note: Phishing is established by researchers (SecureWorks Bit.ly trail). No source confirms Powell typed a password or lacked 2FA; Cluley's 2FA remark is speculation written before the Bit.ly link was found. Do not claim password-only without extra evidence; consider dropping or labelling provisional.

midnight.name: Password-only smishing
midnight.victimAction: Submit a password after a text-message lure
midnight.note: Documented real smishing campaigns (Smishing Triad toll/USPS lures) harvest card data plus an OTP, i.e. an extra factor, so they belong at Twilight, not Midnight. I found no read-and-confirmed campaign where a victim gave only a password after a text lure. A McAfee 2017 US banking-smishing post surfaced in search but its page timed out and was not read, so it is an unverified lead only. Recommend reclassifying to Twilight or dropping.

midnight.name: Password-only quishing
midnight.victimAction: Submit a password after a QR-code lure (no attachment)
midnight.note: Real quishing campaigns I could read (Sophos incident, Cyble Scanception) are adversary-in-the-middle and capture MFA, so they are Twilight. No documented password-only quishing case found. Recommend reclassifying to Twilight or dropping. The AT&T SOC quishing post returned HTTP 503 and was not read.

abyss.name: Operation Aurora (IE vulnerability)
abyss.victimAction: Visit a malicious web page (link delivery route not publicly determined)

abyss.name: Great Cannon
abyss.victimAction: Visit a page that recruits the browser into DDoS traffic (browser-owner perspective; GitHub, the target, is separate)

abyss.name: Polyfill.io
abyss.victimAction: Load a website containing the compromised third-party script

abyss.name: Cambridge Analytica
abyss.victimAction: A quiz participant authorises a Facebook app to access profile data (friends' data was taken without their action)

abyss.name: UNC6040 / UNC6240 Salesforce campaigns
abyss.victimAction: Approve a malicious connected app, followed by data theft and extortion

abyss.name: Approval-only wallet drainers
abyss.victimAction: Sign a malicious token-approval transaction on a fake dApp page (no seed phrase disclosed)

abyss.name: Pegasus / Trident (link-delivered variant)
abyss.victimAction: Tap a link in a text message (single-click exploit chain; the documented target, Ahmed Mansoor, did not click, so no victim click is documented in this case)
abyss.note: The exploit is link-delivered and needs one click, but Citizen Lab's own test, not a victim, triggered infection. The same report notes WAP Push can open a link with no click. The 2016 case documents a delivery attempt, not a victim action. Keep only with wording that makes this clear, or move to an incident with a confirmed click.

abyss.name: Ledger Connect Kit
abyss.victimAction: Sign a malicious draining transaction (no recovery phrase disclosed)

abyss.name: LockBit 3.0 (drive-by-compromise variant)
abyss.victimAction: Visit a compromised website (technique-level only; no named LockBit 3.0 incident is documented)
abyss.note: CISA lists drive-by compromise (T1189) as one affiliate initial-access technique among RDP, phishing, valid accounts and exploitation. This is a generic technique table: no incident, no detail on whether the drive-by needed further user interaction. Year 2022 is not stated in the page I read. Thin evidence for a main-list entry.

trench.name: SIM swapping
trench.victimAction: None by the subscriber; the carrier is deceived, bribed or breached instead (subscriber perspective; the carrier employee is the deceived party)
trench.note: Subscriber-side no-response holds only for the impersonation, insider and carrier-phishing variants; the carrier employee is the one deceived (IC3 lists all three). Sources do not rule out that the attacker first harvested the subscriber's personal data by other means, so keep the 'subscriber perspective' label. No single year: FBI data covers 2018-2021 and the FCC rule is 2023.

trench.name: Heartbleed
trench.victimAction: None; the service's OpenSSL library discloses memory to any remote requester (users' credentials leak without their involvement)

trench.name: Mirai
trench.victimAction: None; internet-facing devices still on default credentials are infected by automated scanning, with no action by the owner

trench.name: ASUS ShadowHammer
trench.victimAction: None by the user; the backdoored update was delivered by the vendor's own automatic updater (the compromised vendor is the primary victim)
trench.note: Two perspectives: the user took no fresh action (CERT-EU: software 'automatically updated'), but the real victim is ASUS, whose servers and signing certificates were abused (Securelist: malicious updaters 'hosted on the official' ASUS update servers). Securelist says 'downloaded and installed' and does not state whether a prompt appeared, so 'no prompt' is my inference. Attack ran Jun-Nov 2018; it was found Jan 2019 and disclosed Mar 2019, so 2019 works as the incident year. ASUS's own statement page did not load content, so it is not cited.

trench.name: MOVEit Transfer
trench.victimAction: None; the file-transfer server was exploited through an unauthenticated web flaw and its data stolen (organisation and data-subject perspectives)

trench.name: WannaCry
trench.victimAction: None; the worm spreads between unpatched Windows machines over SMBv1 (first-infection route not confirmed)

trench.name: SQL Slammer
trench.victimAction: None; a single UDP packet to an exposed SQL Server infects it, with no response needed from the victim

trench.name: Blaster
trench.victimAction: None; the worm exploits the Windows RPC/DCOM service and spreads without user action

trench.name: Sasser
trench.victimAction: None; the worm scans for and exploits the Windows LSASS flaw (MS04-011) on its own

trench.name: Conficker (network-service variant)
trench.victimAction: None (network-service variant only); unpatched Windows Server-service hosts are exploited remotely. USB and share routes are separate

trench.name: Equifax (Struts exploitation)
trench.victimAction: None by the affected individuals; Equifax's internet-facing dispute portal was breached through a known Apache Struts flaw (the company's patching failure, not a response to a lure)
trench.note: Individuals (at least 145.5M per GAO) did nothing, so this holds from their view. From Equifax's view it was a missed patch: the same press release says Equifax's Security organization 'was aware of this vulnerability' in March 2017. That is organisational omission, not a fresh response to a lure. No exploit-chain document was fetched beyond these; the Senate and House reports were seen in search results only and are not cited.

trench.name: Log4Shell (server-side exploitation)
trench.victimAction: None; a crafted request to a vulnerable server makes it run attacker code
